OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $N\geq 1$. What is the largest $t$ such that there are $A_1,\ldots,A_t\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $A_i\cap A_j$ a non-empty arithmetic progression for all $i\neq j$?
#272: [ErGr80,p.20]
additive combinatorics | 
arithmetic progressions
Simonovits and Sós [SiSo81] have shown that $t\ll N^2$.
Erdős and Graham asked whether the maximal $t$ is achieved when we take the $A_i$ to be all arithmetic progressions in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing some fixed element, 'presumably the integer $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$'. This was disproved by Simonovits and Sós [SiSo81], who observed that taking all sets containing at most $3$ elements, containing some fixed element, produces $\binom{N}{2}+1$ many such sets, which is asymptotically greater than the number of arithmetic progressions containing a fixed element, which is $\sim \frac{\pi^2}{24}N^2$.
If we drop the non-empty requirement then Graham, Simonovits, and Sós [GSS80] have shown that\[t\leq \binom{N}{3}+\binom{N}{2}+\binom{N}{1}+1\]and this is best possible.
Szabo [Sz99] proved that the maximal such $t$ is equal to\[\frac{N^2}{2}+O(N^{5/3}(\log N)^3),\]resolving the asymptotic question. On the other hand, Szabo showed that the conjecture of Simonovits and Sós that $\binom{n}{2}+1$ is best possible is false, giving a construction which yields\[t \geq \binom{N}{2}+\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{4}\right\rfloor+1.\]Szabo conjectures that the asymptotic $t=\binom{N}{2}+O(N)$ holds, and that in any extremal example there is an integer contained in all sets.
Additional thanks to: Stijn Cambie, Zach Hunter and Desmond Weisenberg

 Update on a potential conjecture and verification for small numbers:
For $1 \le N \le 9$ (verified fully) and $10 \le N \le 14$ (assuming there is a singleton set $\{c\}$ in the extremal family), the extrema for $t$ are $\binom{N}{2}+\lceil N/4 \rceil.$
These values correspond with the ones by the construction (end of paper) by [Szabo99].
For $N=13$, there are $5$ extremal families all containing $7$.
(Szabo also mentioned his construction can be tweaked in multiple ways)

 Reducing the number of comments, in conclusion:
The conjectures of Erdos and Graham, as well as Simonovits and Sós are both false.
The state of the art (based on its references in Google Scholar) is the work 
[Szabo99].
In particular, here it is proven (theorem 2.1) that $t \le (1+o(1)\frac {N^2}{2}$.
Here, two questions are presented at the end:
*Can one prove that every element of an
extremal system contains a fixed integer $c$?
*It is true that $t \le \frac {N^2}{2}+O(N)?$
(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

At the bottom of page 364, they point out that you can take all the sets of three or fewer elements where one of the elements is fixed. This yields $\binom{n}{2} + 1$ sets. They conjecture that this is the largest possible, and give some minor variants just before the end of the paper.

 I now have also done some computations for small N.
For fixed $N$, given the maximum value of $t$, there may be multiple families $\mathcal F= \{A_1, \ldots, A_t\}$ attaining equality.
For $N=4$, there are $4$ ($14$ if not considered up to isomorphism) families with $t=7$.
Two families with one element in common
*[{3}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}, {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}, {1, 2, 3, 4}]
*[{1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 4}, {1, 3, 4}]
Two families have no element in common:
*[{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 4}, {1, 3, 4}, {2, 3, 4}]
*[{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 4}, {1, 3, 4}, {2, 3, 4}]
For $N=5$, only the conjectured family by Erdos and Graham with $k=3$.
For $N=6$, there is only one extremal family up to isomorphism
[{3}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}, {3, 5}, {3, 6},
 {1, 2, 3}, {1, 3, 5}, {1, 3, 6}, {2, 3, 4}, {2, 3, 6}, {3, 4, 5},
 {3, 4, 6},{3, 5, 6}, {1, 2, 3, 4}, {2, 3, 4, 5}, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}]
(so already not of the conjectured form)
For $3 \le N \le 9$, the extrema are resp. $$\textbf{4},\textbf{7},\textbf{12},17,23,30,\textbf{39}$$
(bolt values are examples where the maximum is attained by, possibly among others, a family of arithmetic progressions containing some fixed element)

 To clarify, Erdős and Graham made two separate conjectures: they conjectured that $t$ is maximized when we take the $A_i$ to be the arithmetic progressions containing some fixed element, and they conjectured that the amount of sets in this construction is maximized when the fixed element is $\left\lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right\rfloor$. (Though perhaps they meant to say $\left\lceil \frac{N}{2} \right\rceil$?) If the fixed element is $k$, then the amount of progressions is
\begin{equation*}
\left(\sum_{d=1}^{N-1}\left\lceil\frac{k}{d}\right\rceil\left\lceil\frac{N-k+1}{d}\right\rceil\right) - N + 2.
\end{equation*}
In the above expression, the variable $d$ represents the difference of the progression, and the subtraction is to account for the fact that the singleton set is counted multiple times.

 Since $\frac{N+1}{2}$ is the central element, $\lceil N/2 \rceil =\lfloor (N+1)/2 \rfloor$ would indeed be more natural, maximizing the main term where $d=1$.
Nevertheless, the second conjecture is also false. The rounding has a big impact ($k-1$ having many prime factors should be advantageous, since rounding up $k/d$ implies the other factor is taken once more)
E.g., when $N=29$, the optimum is attained in $k=13$ (and symmetrically in $k=17$).
